newsitem.title: UK: Injuries in sectarian brawl before N.Irish match.
newsitem.headline: Injuries in sectarian brawl before N.Irish match.

text.p: Five police officers and several civilians were hurt when Protestant soccer fans attacked two busloads of Roman Catholic supporters of a rival club in Northern Ireland on Saturday.
The clashes happened outside a football ground in Portadown, a staunchly pro-British town, 25 miles (40 km) southwest of Belfast, the Northern Ireland capital.
The match between Portadown and Cliftonville, a predominantly Roman Catholic area of Belfast, was halted at half-time, with the home team trailing 0-1.
"Buses carrying Cliftonville supporters...were attacked by a section of a crowd who had mounted a protest outside the ground," a Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) police spokesman say.
"Bottles and other missiles were thrown and police intervened to disperse the crowd."

Northern Ireland has been on edge since sectarian violence in July and August over parades by the Protestant, pro-British Orange Order. The bombing of Britain's Northern Ireland army base by Irish Republican Army guerrillas two weeks ago also raised tension.
Cliftonville fans were prevented by Protestants last month from reaching the Oval ground for a cup tie in East Belfast.
Two of their matches this season have been brought forward because of concern about possible violence.
Chief Superintendent Bill McCreesh, RUC commander in the Portadown district, issued a statement condemning Saturday's attackers as "vicious thugs".
Police said windows on the coaches had been broken. Eyewitnesses said fans on the coaches had to use seats to shield themselves from the missiles.
Liam Murray, secretary of Glenpark Reds, one of Cliftonville's main supporters groups, said they had been attacked for up to 20 minutes.
He said: "It was sheer hatred. There was sheer hatred in their faces. I have never seen anything like that before. It was unbelievable."

Cliftonville chairman Jim Boyce said his club was being victimised. "It is becoming very, very serious," he told the British Broadcasting Corporation. "Football and sport should be kept completely different from any political problems."
